analysis.body:
Federal agencies are in the early stages of deploying artificial intelligence, with adoption concentrated in specific high-value use cases but most projects still in planning rather than production. According to the GAO, twenty of twenty-three agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, with NASA and the Department of Commerce reporting the highest number. These agencies are applying AI to analyze drone photographs, process camera and radar data to identify border activities, and target scientific specimens for planetary rovers. However, most reported use cases remain in planning phase, with only about 200 instances of AI actually in production across the federal government. This suggests that despite significant interest, operational deployment remains limited.

The federal government is investing substantially in AI capability but lacks coordinated governance to manage deployment consistently. The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI. Yet the GAO found that ten of twenty-three agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, while twelve implemented some but not all. Critical gaps include the absence of government-wide guidance on AI acquisition and use, failure of the Office of Management and Budget to develop such guidance, and inconsistent data quality in agency inventories, with five of twenty agencies providing comprehensive information while fifteen had instances of incomplete or inaccurate reporting. The Office of Science and Technology Policy also did not communicate its designation of which agencies were expected to fulfill specific AI requirements, creating confusion across the federal system.

Data quality and risk management present substantial operational challenges. GAO analysis identified instances where some agency inventories lacked required data elements such as AI lifecycle stage or whether systems were releasable, and two inventories included uses later determined by agencies not to be AI at all. Without accurate inventories, the government's management of AI use will be hindered. The GAO notes that while AI poses risks that can negatively impact individuals, groups, organizations, communities, and society, federal agencies have taken only initial steps to comply with requirements in executive orders and federal law, with more work remaining to fully implement safeguards needed to manage AI risks.

International frameworks and regulatory tracking reveal growing policy attention to government AI but wide variation in readiness. The OECD.AI Policy Observatory tracks over 900 national AI policies and initiatives while promoting trustworthy AI aligned with OECD AI Principles. Oxford Insights ranks national readiness across policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption. Stanford HAI's AI Index measures government AI through legislation counts, national strategy execution, and public-sector procurement as part of its annual comprehensive assessment of AI's technical progress and societal impact. This ecosystem of independent measurement reflects recognition that government adoption of AI requires coordinated policy frameworks and transparent reporting.

For government agencies considering AI deployment, the evidence points to clear prerequisites before scaling. GAO's findings show that Commerce and the General Services Administration have made progress by establishing technical standards development and an AI Center of Excellence respectively, but these remain exceptions rather than benchmarks across the federal system. Any agency planning significant AI use should expect to invest in inventory accuracy, assign clear roles for AI work through updated occupational categories, and align deployment with government-wide guidance once developed. The gap between planned and operational use cases suggests that successful implementation requires infrastructure and governance maturity that most agencies have yet to establish.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI is a policy observatory that maintains a database of over 900 national AI policies and initiatives, alongside live AI data and policy analysis. The platform promotes the OECD AI Principles to help countries develop trustworthy AI systems, and invites organisations developing advanced AI to submit reports on their risk mitigation measures to improve transparency and comparability. In July 2024, the GPAI initiative merged with OECD member countries' AI work under the GPAI brand to form an integrated partnership. The observatory aims to support AI actors in building systems that respect human rights, fairness, transparency, explainability, robustness, and security.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-laws/.brief: The page reports that 4,360 AI bills are tracked across 53 U.S. jurisdictions, with daily updates from LegiScan. It also lists books by Stephen R. Jordan, including the “Operating Discipline for AI Library™” series. Additionally, the page mentions several AI audit services such as the AI Business Enablement Audit™ and the AI Risk & Governance Review™.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
